title: How to study this course
standfirst: Physiology is not a memorization subject, and studying it like one is the single most common reason people who work hard still do badly. Here is what works instead.

p: Rereading feels like studying. The page gets more familiar every time you go over it, and your brain reads that familiarity as knowing. It is not the same thing, and the gap between them is where grades disappear.

The test of whether you know something is whether you can produce it with the book closed. Not recognize it. Produce it. Everything in this course is built around making you do that early, while there is still time to fix what is missing.
sections.callout: If your study session did not involve a blank page at some point, it was reading, not studying.

p: The order matters more than the effort. Trying to remember something and failing does more for your memory than reading the right answer straight away, which is why every assignment here asks you to attempt it before you look.
steps: Close the book. Write or draw what you know about the topic.
Notice what you could not produce. That gap is the entire point of the exercise.
*Now* open the book and correct what you wrote, in a different color so the gap stays visible.
Look at the corrections a few days later. Those are the things worth another pass.
sections.callout: A wrong first attempt that you caught and corrected is worth more than a perfect page copied with the book open.

p: Almost everything in this course is a relationship with a direction. Pressure goes up, so flow goes up. Potassium leaves, so the membrane potential falls. You can write a sentence about baroreceptors without knowing which way anything goes, but you cannot draw the loop without committing to a direction.
That is why the chart entry is a drawing rather than a paragraph. The drawing forces the commitment that words let you dodge.

sections.h: Spacing beats cramming, and it is not close
p: Four twenty minute sessions across a week beat one eighty minute session the night before, for the same total time. The recall cards are built to space themselves, so the simplest version of this advice is to open them for fifteen minutes most days rather than for two hours once.
list: Most days, fifteen minutes of recall cards.
Once a week, one drawing from memory with the book shut.
Before an exam, redo the drawings you got wrong the first time, not the ones you got right.

p: AI is allowed on a lot of the work here and it is genuinely useful, but only in one direction: as a tutor after you have tried, not as an oracle instead of trying.

The problem log enforces the order, and the reason is not suspicion. It is that a problem you watched someone else solve leaves almost nothing behind, and in Week 8 you will be solving one on a whiteboard with a timer running and nothing open.
sections.callout: Ask it why your answer was wrong. Do not ask it what the answer is.

sections.h: What to do when you are lost
p: Being lost in physiology usually means a missing piece from three weeks earlier rather than a failure to understand today. The competency list is there so you can find which piece.
list: Open the week page and read the competency list for the topic that is confusing you.
Find the earliest one you cannot do, and go back to that week.
If it is an anatomy gap, use the anatomy review page. You are not behind, this course does not assume you took anatomy.
If none of that works, ask me. Early is a small question. Late is a large one.
